'''Brian Scarlett''' (11 July 1938 – 2 September 2004) was an English physicist and academic specialising in [[particle technology]].

==Early life and education==
Scarlett was born on 11 July 1938 in [[Biddulph]], [[Staffordshire]], [[England]].<ref name=Davies1>{{cite journal |last=Davies |first=Reg |title=In Memoriam: Professor Brian Scarlett |journal=Particle & Particle Systems Characterization |volume=21 |year=2004 |pages=177–178}}</ref><ref name=Davies2>{{cite magazine |last=Davies |first=Reg |title=Brian Scarlett Remembered |url=https://www.aiche.org/sites/default/files/community/498601/aiche-community-site-newsletter/498876/2004fallptfnewsletter.pdf |magazine=Particle Technology Forum Newsletter |publisher=American Institute of Chemical Engineers |date=Fall 2004 |pages=3–4 |access-date=25 August 2026}}</ref>
He attended [[Wolstanton High School|Wolstanton Grammar School]] and the [[University of Durham]], graduating with a BSc in physics in 1959.<ref>{{cite journal |title=Supplement to the Graduate List Last Published in 1954 |journal=Graduates of the University |date=1960 |page=108 |url=http://reed.dur.ac.uk/xtf/view?docId=bookreader/DU_Calendars/DurhamGraduates/DurhamGraduatesMETSfile.xml#page/374/mode/2up |access-date=11 January 2021}}</ref> He completed a M.Sc. degree from the same institution in 1964.<ref>{{cite journal |title=Physics |journal=Report by the Vice-Chancellor and Warden for the Year 1964-65 |date=1965 |page=72 |url=https://reed.dur.ac.uk/xtf/view?docId=bookreader/DU_Warden/warden64/wr1964METSfile.xml#page/76/mode/2up |access-date=3 July 2022 |publisher=Durham University}}</ref><ref>{{cite thesis |last=Scarlett |first=Brian |title=The Effective Thermal Conductivity of Packed Beds of Metal Powder |type=MSc thesis |publisher=Durham University |year=1964 |url=https://etheses.dur.ac.uk/10458/1/10458_7255.PDF |access-date=25 August 2026}}</ref>

==Career==
In 1964, he joined the [[United Kingdom Atomic Energy Authority]], and was based at [[Chapelcross nuclear power station]] in [[Annan, Dumfries and Galloway|Annan]].<ref name=Davies2/> Two years later he obtained a research assistantship at the [[Nottingham Trent University|Nottingham and District Technical College]], where he was first introduced to the subject of particle technology. He moved to the Department of Chemical Engineering at [[Loughborough University of Technology]] in 1969, becoming leader of the particle technology group and senior lecturer.<ref name=Davies1/><ref name=Davies2/>

While at Loughborough, Scarlett served as a [[local councillor]] for [[Borough of Charnwood|Charnwood District Council]] and was appointed to represent [[Leicestershire County Council]] on the [[Trent River Authority]], where he rose to the position of Chairman of Water Management.  He contemplated a full-time career in politics, but decided to stay as an academic.<ref name=Davies1/>

In 1983, Scarlett was appointed professor of chemical technology at [[Delft University of Technology]]. His inaugural lecture set out his conception of particle technology as a multidisciplinary field, emphasising the importance of particle characterisation and the standardisation of particle-analysis techniques.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Scarlett |first=Brian |title=Particle Technology – Manipulating the Divided |journal=Particle & Particle Systems Characterization |year=1984 |volume=1 |issue=1–4 |pages=1–6 |doi=10.1002/ppsc.19840010101}}</ref> He led a large research group at Delft, supervising around 50 doctoral and nearly 150 master's and engineering theses.<ref name=Davies2/>

In 1990, he moved to the [[University of Florida]] as full professor in the [[National Science Foundation]] Engineering Research Centre, in particle science and technology, forming the largest academic group in powder mechanics in the US.<ref name=Davies1/><ref name=Davies2/>

Scarlett was also involved in developing standards for particle measurement and served as chairman of the [[International Organization for Standardization|ISO]] technical committee concerned with particle characterisation.<ref name="Davies1" /> During his career, he produced around 350 publications and conference presentations.<ref name=Davies2/>

==Personal life==
Scarlett's dress sense was "very conservative" and, despite the hot climate, he exclusively wore suits and ties during his period working at the University of Florida.<ref name=Davies2/>

Scarlett died on 2 September 2004 in [[Gainesville, Florida|Gainesville]], Florida. He was survived by his wife Joan, son Ian, and daughters Diane and Judy.<ref name=Davies1/><ref name=Davies2/>

==Honours==
Scarlett was a [[Fellow of the Royal Academy of Engineering]], a Fellow of the [[Institute of Physics]], and a Fellow of the [[Institution of Chemical Engineers]].  He was awarded honorary doctorates (DSc) by the [[University of Coimbra]] (1997) and Loughborough University (1999).<ref name=Davies2/>
